title: Inconsistent enforcement between per-key / per-org / per-route quotas leading to metering drift
creator: Liam Chen
description:
Summary:
Production reports and internal audits show mismatches between the tokens/requests charged on invoices and the actual requests denied by the rate-limiter. Root cause appears to be inconsistent application of rate limit policies when multiple scopes are present (per-key, per-org, per-route) and when requests hit fallback model variants. Symptoms include: customers seeing usage spikes on billing dashboards without corresponding successful requests in the logs; some clients receiving 429s while their billing counters still increment; other clients not incrementing quotas when they should (leading to silent overage).

Why this matters:
- Potential revenue and customer trust impact (overcharging or under-enforcing quotas).
- Incorrect enforcement undermines SLA and quota guarantees for Dedicated/Private customers.

Observed behavior (examples):
1) Request A: API key K1 calls route /v1/generate with model M-quant. Due to kernel-compat fallback we route to M-compat. Rate limiter logs: "rate_limit.check: OK per-key K1, OK per-org O17, DENY per-route /v1/generate -> DENY_REASON:route_quota". Billing meter: increments token count for K1 by 512 even though response was 429.
2) Request B: Burst of concurrent streaming requests from org O22. Serving runtime returns partial 206 then final 429 from route quota. Billing shows no increments for O22; customer reports being able to produce more tokens than quota.

Hypothesis:
- Policy evaluation order and the billing increment call are decoupled. In some code paths we increment usage pre-enforcement (race with enforcement decision). In other code paths we never call increment when enforcement short-circuits earlier (e.g., when routed to fallback code path).
- Caching layer (prefix/KV cache) sometimes proxies responses to the client while bypassing the centralized usage increment due to local fast-paths.

Repro steps (dev env):
1) Use org O-Test and API key K-Test with per-route quota 1000 tokens/day, per-key 500 tokens/day.
2) Send a scripted burst of 50 parallel requests with 30 tokens each to /v1/generate while toggling the route limit low.
3) Observe: some requests return 429 but billing counters in MySQL are incremented; some requests succeed while counters are not incremented.
4) Check metrics: rate_limit.enforcement.latency, billing.increment.errors, billing.charge.delta.

Logs (redacted):
- [2026-03-02T14:12:05Z] rate-limit: eval order [per-org, per-route, per-key], result {per-org:OK, per-route:DENY, per-key:OK}
- [2026-03-02T14:12:05Z] billing: increment called key=K1 tokens=512 trace=abc123 result=OK
- [2026-03-02T14:12:05Z] http: response 429 body="route quota exceeded" trace=abc123

Initial triage and temporary mitigations applied:
- Rolled config change to force synchronous billing increment after enforcement decision for hosted traffic only (hotfix r1103). Reduced inconsistent increments in canary region but not full plateau.
- Increased sampling and added 1% detailed tracing for rate-limit decision paths and billing increments.

Work to do (this ticket):
1) Fix core race: unify policy evaluation and usage increment into a single transactional path or introduce a single authoritative enforcement service. (ENG-8931 to refactor policy engine call sites)
2) Ensure fallback model routing preserves the enforcement metadata and propagates enforcement outcome to billing component (ENG-8932 to add propagation hooks).
3) Audit local fast-paths and KV/prefix cache layer to ensure they call centralized billing increment or emit compensating events.
4) Build a deterministic unit + integration test harness that simulates concurrent enforcement and billing under different evaluation orders.
5) Create migration/repair job to reconcile billing counters vs. request logs for last 30 days with safe adjustments and customer-facing remediation plan.

Acceptance criteria:
- All request paths (hosted, dedicated, private) either increment usage only after an affirmative allow decision or reliably emit a compensating decrement when an initial increment was performed and the final decision is deny.
- End-to-end test coverage demonstrating no more than 0.01% disagreement in a 1M request synthetic workload between enforcement decisions and billing increments.
- Post-deploy reconciliation job with dry-run report and stakeholder sign-off.

Rollout plan:
- Merge patch to feature branch behind a feature flag. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1543)
- Canary in us-west-2 on hosted API for 24 hours with aggressive sampling and customer-monitoring alerting enabled.
- Expand to all hosted regions if canary shows <0.005% disagreement for 24h.
- For Dedicated/Private: ship agent library update with feature flag + guide for customers to opt-in; coordinate with solutions engineering for staged rollouts.

Open design questions / trade-offs considered:
- Option A: Move to centralized enforcement microservice (single source of truth). Pros: correctness, easier audits. Cons: increased round-trip latency and single point of failure unless replicated.
- Option B: Tighten local fast-paths with strict propagation hooks and a lightweight consensus/increment protocol. Pros: lower latency, less architectural change. Cons: more complex correctness proofs, requires more integration tests.

Decision so far: proceed with Option B as a short-to-medium term fix (lower latency impact) while prototyping Option A as a long-term architectural goal. Detailed design in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Rate+Limit+Policy+Engine+Correctness

Estimate and timeline:
- Refactor and tests (ENG-8931): 5 dev days
- Propagation hooks and cache audit (ENG-8932): 3 dev days
- Reconciliation tooling and dry-run: 2 dev days
- Total: 10 dev days including review and canary monitoring.
